gray-wolf.hook: Still widespread in the far north, after vanishing from much of Europe and the United States.
gray-wolf.imageAlt: A gray wolf standing in snow, looking toward the camera
gray-wolf.what: The gray wolf is a large social canid and the wild ancestor of the domestic dog. Packs hunt ungulates and also take smaller prey. Globally the species is listed as Least Concern because large numbers remain in Canada, Russia, and Central Asia.
gray-wolf.range: Historically most of the Northern Hemisphere. Today the strongholds are boreal and steppe Asia, Canada, and Alaska, with recovering fragments in Europe and a few reintroduction areas in the contiguous United States and Mexico.
gray-wolf.story: In the last few centuries people shot, poisoned, and trapped wolves as livestock enemies. They disappeared from most of Western Europe and from almost all of the contiguous United States by the early 1900s. Legal protection and reintroductions (Yellowstone, the northern Rockies, parts of Europe) have brought some populations back. The Holocene picture: wolves across temperate forests and plains: is still only partly restored.
gray-wolf.when: Still here. Range and numbers contracted sharply under persecution, then rose again where hunting was limited.
gray-wolf.humanRole: Deliberate killing and habitat loss removed wolves from settled landscapes; later law and reintroduction put some of them back.
gray-wolf.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Canis lupus, Least Concern); recovery reviews for Europe and North America.

brown-bear.hook: A Holarctic survivor whose European range is now a scatter of mountain and forest remnants.
brown-bear.imageAlt: A brown bear running across mossy ground
brown-bear.what: The brown bear is the most widespread bear, from coastal salmon rivers to dry mountains. IUCN lists it as Least Concern. Size and diet vary by region; the Eurasian brown bear and the North American grizzly and Kodiak are the same species.
brown-bear.range: Once across Europe, northern Asia, and western North America. Large populations remain in Russia, Scandinavia, the Carpathians, the Balkans, Alaska, and western Canada. Most of Western and Central Europe lost theirs.
brown-bear.story: Hunting and the clearing of lowland forest pushed brown bears into mountains and remote taiga. A few Alpine and Pyrenean groups hang on or are being reinforced. The species is not globally rare, but the Holocene map: bears following Ice Age prey into newly opened Europe: is not the map of today.
brown-bear.when: Still here. Locally extinct across much of temperate Europe; stable or increasing where people tolerate them.
brown-bear.humanRole: Hunting and farmland removed bears from settled Europe; remaining populations persist on human sufferance.
brown-bear.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Ursus arctos, Least Concern); European large-carnivore status reports.

american-bison.hook: From tens of millions on the Great Plains to a few hundred by the 1880s, then a managed return.
american-bison.imageAlt: An American bison standing in dry grass
american-bison.what: The American bison is a heavy grazing bovine of North American grasslands. IUCN lists it as Near Threatened. Most animals alive today are in commercial herds; conservation herds that are managed as wildlife are much smaller.
american-bison.range: Once from northern Mexico through the Great Plains into Canada. Wild or semi-wild herds now occupy scattered parks and reserves; the species no longer moves as a continental migrant.
american-bison.story: Indigenous nations hunted bison for millennia without collapsing the species. Nineteenth-century market hunting, railroads, and U.S. campaign policy reduced the plains population from an estimated tens of millions to a few hundred by the 1880s. Ranching and park herds then rebuilt numbers. The animal survived; the free-ranging ecology did not.
american-bison.when: Still here, mostly as a managed animal. IUCN Near Threatened.
american-bison.humanRole: Industrial hunting and settlement almost erased it; later ranching and reserves kept a remnant.
american-bison.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Bison bison, Near Threatened); historical plains-bison estimates (order-of-magnitude).

african-savanna-elephant.hook: Still the largest land animal: listed Endangered in 2021 after decades of ivory and habitat loss.
african-savanna-elephant.imageAlt: An African savanna elephant walking through dry bush
african-savanna-elephant.what: The African savanna elephant is one of two living African elephant species, separated from the forest elephant on the IUCN Red List in 2021 and listed Endangered. It shapes woodland and grassland by browsing and by opening water.
african-savanna-elephant.range: Eastern and southern Africa hold the largest remaining populations. It is gone or reduced to fragments in much of West Africa and in many former savannas.
african-savanna-elephant.story: People have hunted elephants for ivory for centuries; industrial poaching in the late twentieth century, plus farms and fences, cut the range. The 2021 IUCN assessment estimated a decline of more than 60 percent over three generations. Southern African parks still hold large herds. That is survival, not the Holocene distribution.
african-savanna-elephant.when: Still here, and Endangered. Numbers and range are a fraction of the Holocene picture.
african-savanna-elephant.humanRole: Ivory markets and expanding settlement are the main recent pressures; both continue.
african-savanna-elephant.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Loxodonta africana, Endangered, 2021); IUCN African Elephant Specialist Group.

lion.hook: Gone from Europe and almost all of Asia; surviving in African fragments and one Indian forest.
lion.imageAlt: A male lion lying in dry grass in Namibia
lion.what: The lion is a social big cat of open woodlands and savannas. IUCN lists the species as Vulnerable. Published guesses for the wild total often fall around 20,000-25,000; the figure is uncertain and regional counts disagree.
lion.range: Historically from southern Europe and southwest Asia across most of Africa. Today almost all wild lions live in sub-Saharan fragments. The Asiatic lion survives only in and around Gir Forest, India (on the order of 600-700 animals in recent Gujarat counts).
lion.story: Over the last few thousand years, and especially the last two centuries, people converted hunting ground to pasture and shot lions as threats. The Ice Age lion of Europe is long gone; the Holocene lion of North Africa and the Middle East followed. What remains is a reduced African core plus Gir.
lion.when: Still here, Vulnerable, on a much smaller map than after the last Ice Age.
lion.humanRole: Habitat conversion, prey depletion, and killing in defense of livestock drove the contraction.
lion.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Panthera leo, Vulnerable); Gujarat Forest Department Asiatic-lion censuses.

red-deer.hook: A European Ice Age survivor that is now common where forestry and hunting keep it that way.
red-deer.imageAlt: A red deer stag with large antlers standing in a forest clearing
red-deer.what: The red deer is a large Eurasian cervid. IUCN lists it as Least Concern. The North American elk, or wapiti (Cervus canadensis), is a close relative with a parallel story of hunting, clearance, and later recovery in parks.
red-deer.range: Native across Europe and western Asia, with many island and mountain populations. Density now follows hunting law and forestry more than Ice Age steppe and woodland.
red-deer.story: People have hunted red deer since the Late Pleistocene. Forest clearance removed them from some lowlands; elsewhere game parks and modern forestry produced high local densities. Some island subspecies are rare. The species as a whole is not threatened: its geography is anthropogenic.
red-deer.when: Still here and, in much of Europe, numerous under management.
red-deer.humanRole: Hunting and clearance shrank some populations; later gamekeeping increased others.
red-deer.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Cervus elaphus, Least Concern).

wild-boar.hook: Hunted out of some countries, then returned, and became a farmland boom species.
wild-boar.imageAlt: A wild boar standing in a snowy woodland
wild-boar.what: The wild boar is an adaptable omnivorous pig, ancestor of most domestic pigs. IUCN lists it as Least Concern. It roots soil, eats crops, and lives from desert fringe to forest.
wild-boar.range: Native to Eurasia and North Africa. Exterminated in Britain and parts of Scandinavia, then re-established. Introduced and invasive in the Americas, Australia, and many islands.
wild-boar.story: For thousands of years people hunted boar and turned forest into fields. In some regions that erased them. In the last century milder winters, maize, and fewer wolves let European numbers surge. Elsewhere releases for hunting created feral problems. Survival here is not scarcity: it is a rearranged ecology.
wild-boar.when: Still here; locally extinct, then over-abundant, depending on the landscape people built.
wild-boar.humanRole: We reduced it, reintroduced it, and then fed its recovery with crops and empty predator niches.
wild-boar.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Sus scrofa, Least Concern); European population-trend reviews.

european-beaver.hook: Hunted to a handful of refuges, then brought back across Europe by reintroduction.
european-beaver.imageAlt: A Eurasian beaver sitting at the edge of a pond
european-beaver.what: The Eurasian beaver is a large nocturnal rodent that dams streams and fells trees. IUCN lists it as Least Concern after a long collapse and a managed recovery. It is a different species from the North American beaver (Castor canadensis).
european-beaver.range: Once from Britain to China along rivers and wetlands. By the early twentieth century only a few thousand survived in scattered European and Asian pockets. Reintroductions have restored it to much of Europe.
european-beaver.story: Fur, castoreum, and meat drove a hunt that nearly ended the species in Europe. Legal protection and releases from the mid-twentieth century onward rebuilt numbers. The early Holocene beaver was an engineer of ice-free rivers; the beaver of today is often a reintroduction on a drained landscape.
european-beaver.when: Still here, and increasing in Europe after a near miss.
european-beaver.humanRole: Overhunting for fur almost finished it; later policy put it back.
european-beaver.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Castor fiber, Least Concern); European reintroduction summaries.

humpback-whale.hook: Industrial whaling removed more than 90 percent of most stocks; many have since rebounded.
humpback-whale.imageAlt: A humpback whale diving, showing its black-and-white tail flukes
humpback-whale.what: The humpback is a long-finned baleen whale that migrates between polar feeding grounds and tropical breeding waters. IUCN listed it as Least Concern in 2018 after several ocean-basin recoveries. Some regional stocks remain small, including the Arabian Sea population.
humpback-whale.range: All oceans. Breeding and feeding sites are traditional; the species is cosmopolitan as a migrant, not as a resident of every coast.
humpback-whale.story: Nineteenth- and twentieth-century commercial whaling cut most populations by more than 90 percent by the 1960s. The international moratorium on commercial whaling (International Whaling Commission, 1982, phased in) allowed many stocks to grow again. Ship strikes and fishing gear still kill animals.
humpback-whale.when: Still here. Globally Least Concern; recovery is real and incomplete.
humpback-whale.humanRole: Industrial hunting caused the crash; a hunting ban, not a change of habitat, allowed the rebound.
humpback-whale.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Megaptera novaeangliae, Least Concern, 2018); IWC whaling history.

european-bison.hook: Wiped out in the wild in the early 1900s, then rebuilt: free-living herds grew from about 1,800 animals in 2003 to 6,244 across 47 subpopulations by 2019, and IUCN moved the species from Vulnerable to Near Threatened.
european-bison.imageAlt: A European bison bull standing in an autumn forest
european-bison.what: Europe’s largest land mammal: a wild cattle relative of the American bison, not the same species. Lowland and highland lines were saved in zoos after the last wild animals were shot, then released back into forests from the 1950s onward.
european-bison.range: Europe. By 2019 free-living animals were back in forests, across 47 subpopulations. Only about eight herds are large enough for long-term genetic viability; most herds stay small and mostly isolated.
european-bison.story: This is a managed comeback after people emptied the range: captive breeding, reintroductions, and ongoing herd management. It is still conservation-dependent (small, mostly isolated herds), not an unthreatened boom like wild boar, but it is back on the landscape.
european-bison.when: IUCN (2020 assessment): free-living population ~1,800 (2003) → 6,244 (2019) in 47 herds. Status: Near Threatened, moved from Vulnerable. A later Oryx note cited roughly 6,800 free-ranging by 2020 as planning continued.
european-bison.humanRole: People shot the last wild animals. Captive breeding, releases into forests from the 1950s, and ongoing herd management put free-living herds back.
european-bison.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Bison bonasus, Near Threatened, 2020); IUCN news, 10 Dec 2020; Oryx range-wide conservation action plan note.

north-american-beaver.hook: Almost erased across much of its range by about 1900 for felt hats; regulated trapping and mid-century reintroductions rebuilt a continent-wide keystone: IUCN now lists it Least Concern, with modern totals commonly estimated in the tens of millions (often ~10-15 million).
north-american-beaver.imageAlt: A North American beaver sitting on a log at the edge of a pond
north-american-beaver.what: The New World dam-builder: same family as the Eurasian beaver already on this shelf, different species. It reshapes streams into wetlands that hold water, store carbon in ponds, and feed other wildlife.
north-american-beaver.range: A continent-wide keystone again, restored where habitat remains, after being almost erased across much of its range. Not the Eurasian beaver (Castor fiber).
north-american-beaver.story: People hunted it to local extinction for fur, then brought it back. Where numbers are high it is now a farmland and road-culvert conflict species: a classic “still here, then boom” Surviving story, not an Endangered rarity.
north-american-beaver.when: By about 1900 beavers were nearly gone from many original habitats. USDA Forest Service Region 2 assessment: harvest rules, wetland protection, translocation, and natural spread restored populations where habitat remains. Modern totals are commonly estimated in the tens of millions (often ~10-15 million). A Stanford summary of recent mapping work cites a drop from rough pre-colonial 60-400 million guesses to about 10-15 million today: treat the historic ceiling as uncertain; the direction (collapse → millions again) is solid. IUCN: Least Concern.
north-american-beaver.humanRole: The fur trade for felt hats nearly erased it. Regulated trapping and mid-century reintroductions rebuilt it.
north-american-beaver.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Castor canadensis, Least Concern); Animal Diversity Web; USDA Forest Service Region 2 assessment; Stanford Report, 11 Aug 2025; Communications Earth & Environment (doi:10.1038/s43247-025-02572-y).

bald-eagle.hook: Down to 417 known nesting pairs in the lower 48 U.S. states in 1963. After the ban on dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane and work under the Endangered Species Act, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service counted about 316,700 individuals and 71,467 occupied nests in the survey for 2018 to 2019.
bald-eagle.imageAlt: An adult bald eagle in flight over water, white head and tail showing
bald-eagle.what: North America’s fish eagle and the national symbol of the United States. It is the only eagle native solely to this continent. Adults show the white head and tail. Younger birds stay mottled brown for years.
bald-eagle.range: North America. The published recovery counts are for the lower 48 states.
bald-eagle.story: Shooting and dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane thinned eggshells until the bird nearly vanished from the contiguous United States. Legal protection, nest-site work, and the 1972 United States ban on that insecticide reversed the crash. The species was removed from the Endangered Species Act list in 2007. It remains protected under the Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act and the Migratory Bird Treaty Act.
bald-eagle.when: The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service recorded 417 known nesting pairs in the lower 48 U.S. states in 1963, then 9,789 pairs at the 2007 delisting, then about 316,700 individuals and 71,467 occupied nests in the 2018 to 2019 data. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists the species as Least Concern.
bald-eagle.humanRole: Shooting and dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane caused the crash. The 1972 ban on that insecticide, Endangered Species Act work, and nest-site protection reversed it.
bald-eagle.sourcesNote: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service bald eagle species page; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Bald Eagle Population Size: 2020 Update; Federal Register delisting rule, 2007.

white-rhinoceros.hook: Southern white rhinos were hunted to a single South African refuge a century ago; IUCN/TRAFFIC now put African white rhinos at about 15,752 at end-2024: Near Threatened, and still the main living white-rhino stock.
white-rhinoceros.imageAlt: A southern white rhinoceros and calf grazing, wide square lip showing
white-rhinoceros.what: The wide-mouthed “square-lipped” grazer of African savanna. Two subspecies: southern (the recovery) and northern (functionally extinct in the wild: already told on the Endangered shelf). Almost all living white rhinos are the southern subspecies (C. s. simum).
white-rhinoceros.range: African savanna. Southern white rhinos were hunted to a single South African refuge a century ago. The northern subspecies is not this card’s hero figure.
white-rhinoceros.story: Protection and translocation from Hluhluwe-iMfolozi rebuilt southern numbers from a tiny remnant into the tens of thousands. That is a Surviving comeback. It is not the same story as Critically Endangered black, Javan, or Sumatran rhinos, and it is not the northern white remnant.
white-rhinoceros.when: IUCN press release (7 Aug 2025, citing the AfRSG/TRAFFIC CITES report): 15,752 white rhinos in Africa at end-2024 (down 11.2% from 2023: drought, survey, and management shocks after earlier gains). IRF/public summaries still frame the long arc as “fewer than 100 in the early 1900s → tens of thousands.” IUCN Red List: Near Threatened.
white-rhinoceros.humanRole: Hunting reduced the southern subspecies to one refuge. Protection and translocation rebuilt the living stock.
white-rhinoceros.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Ceratotherium simum, Near Threatened); IUCN press release, 7 Aug 2025; International Rhino Foundation; Pachyderm AfRSG chair report; South Africa biodiversity management plan for the white rhinoceros.

arabian-oryx.hook: Declared extinct in the wild in the early 1970s, then returned from captive “world herds”; by the 2016 IUCN assessment about 1,220 animals lived wild again (850 mature), and the species became the first to move from Extinct in the Wild back to Vulnerable.
arabian-oryx.imageAlt: An Arabian oryx standing in desert scrub at Uruq Bani Ma’arid, Saudi Arabia
arabian-oryx.what: A white desert antelope with long, nearly straight horns: the smallest Oryx, native to Arabian Peninsula deserts and steppes.
arabian-oryx.range: Arabian Peninsula deserts and steppes. Releases from 1980 onward put animals back in Oman, Saudi Arabia, Israel, the UAE, Jordan and related sites.
arabian-oryx.story: Motorised hunting emptied the last wild herds. Captive breeding and releases from 1980 onward returned animals from captive “world herds.” It is still threatened (habitat, illegal hunting, small wild totals), but it is a documented return from Extinct in the Wild, not a Critically Endangered leftover with no recovery path.
arabian-oryx.when: Declared extinct in the wild in the early 1970s. IUCN SSC Antelope Specialist Group fact sheet (assessment 2016): about 1,220 in the wild (850 mature) and 6,000-7,000 in captivity. Status: Vulnerable: the first species to move from Extinct in the Wild back to Vulnerable. IUCN news (2011) recorded the step down from a higher threat category. Royal Society Open Science (2021) reviews Oman reintroduction genetics.
arabian-oryx.humanRole: Motorised hunting emptied the last wild herds. Captive breeding and releases from 1980 put the species back.
arabian-oryx.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Oryx leucoryx, Vulnerable); IUCN, “A grain of hope in the desert” (2011); IUCN SSC Antelope Specialist Group fact sheet; Royal Society Open Science, 2021.

iberian-lynx.hook: Only 94 Iberian lynx were left in 2002, which made it the most endangered cat on Earth. The 2025 census counted 2,663 in Spain and Portugal.
iberian-lynx.imageAlt: An Iberian lynx in profile, with tufted ears, a ruff of fur on the cheeks and a short tail with a black tip
iberian-lynx.what: The Iberian lynx (Lynx pardinus) is a medium-sized wild cat with a spotted tawny coat, tufted ears, a ruff of fur along the cheeks and a short tail with a black tip. An adult stands about 0.5 m at the shoulder, measures about 0.9 m from nose to tail tip and weighs roughly 6 to 16 kg. It lives only in the Iberian Peninsula and depends on the wild rabbit, its main prey.
iberian-lynx.range: In 2025 the lynx lived in 26 separate areas of Spain and Portugal, and breeding was recorded in 18 of them. Spain held 2,269 animals and Portugal 394. Inside Spain, Castilla-La Mancha had 1,051, Andalusia 885 and Extremadura 302, with smaller numbers in Murcia, Castilla y León and Madrid. The Sierra Morena mountains are the main stronghold, with 1,145. The regional government of Andalusia counts its lynx up from 457 in 2019 to 885 in 2025. The area where the lynx occurs has grown from 449 square kilometres in 2005 to at least 3,320 in 2022.
iberian-lynx.story: During the twentieth century the Iberian lynx declined for four reasons: its Mediterranean forest was destroyed, two new viral diseases sharply reduced the number of wild rabbits, people hunted it as vermin, and many animals died on roads or drowned in wells. By 2002 only two groups were left, one around Doñana and one in the Sierra Morena mountains, with 94 lynx in total. The species was then recognised as the most endangered cat on Earth, and the International Union for Conservation of Nature rated it Critically Endangered. Spain, Portugal and the European Union began a long rescue. Landowners agreed to manage land so that rabbits could increase, breeding centres in Spain and Portugal raised lynx, and since 2010 more than 400 animals have been released into places where the species had disappeared. Portugal began its own releases in 2014. The total passed 1,000 in 2020 and 2,000 in 2023.
iberian-lynx.when: In June 2024 the International Union for Conservation of Nature moved the Iberian lynx from Endangered to Vulnerable. Before that it was rated Critically Endangered from 2002 to 2008 and Endangered in 2015. The census published in June 2026 by the Spanish Ministry for the Ecological Transition and the Demographic Challenge counted 2,663 lynx in 2025, against 2,401 in 2024 and 1,365 in 2021. Of these, 1,711 were adults and subadults and 952 were cubs, and 542 females were breeding or holding territories. The ministry treats these figures as a minimum.
iberian-lynx.humanRole: People first pushed the lynx to the brink, then helped it back. Agreements with landowners improved habitat and increased rabbit numbers, lynx were bred in centres in Spain and Portugal and released in new areas, and underpasses and fences were built along roads. Roads remain the greatest danger: in 2025, 212 of the 273 recorded lynx deaths happened on roads. The International Union for Conservation of Nature also names new rabbit virus outbreaks, diseases from domestic cats, poaching and climate-related changes to habitat as threats.

black-footed-ferret.hook: North America's only native ferret, once thought extinct and saved from a last few wild animals.
black-footed-ferret.imageAlt: A black-footed ferret with a dark mask peering out over dry grass
black-footed-ferret.what: The black-footed ferret (Mustela nigripes) is a slim weasel of the North American prairie with a pale buff coat, a black mask across the eyes and black feet. Prairie dogs make up most of its food, and it lives in their burrows. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists it as Endangered.
black-footed-ferret.range: Once the Great Plains from southern Canada to northern Mexico, now reintroduced colonies in Wyoming, South Dakota, Montana and Arizona.
black-footed-ferret.story: Black-footed ferrets were thought to be extinct until a ranch dog brought a dead one home near Meeteetse, Wyoming, in 1981. That last wild colony was then hit by plague and distemper, and between 1985 and 1987 the survivors were caught to start a breeding programme. Young ferrets from the programme have been released ever since, about 4,500 so far.
black-footed-ferret.when: Endangered now, living wild only where it has been released.
black-footed-ferret.humanRole: Loss of the prairie dog colonies it needs for food and shelter, and the diseases plague and distemper, threaten it.

golden-lion-tamarin.hook: A tiny golden monkey of Brazil's coastal forest, brought back from about two hundred animals.
golden-lion-tamarin.imageAlt: A golden lion tamarin with a shining orange mane sitting on a branch
golden-lion-tamarin.what: The golden lion tamarin (Leontopithecus rosalia) is a small monkey with long, bright reddish gold fur and a mane around its face. It lives in family groups high in the trees and uses long fingers with claw like nails to search bark and leaves for insects. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists it as Endangered.
golden-lion-tamarin.range: Lowland Atlantic coastal forest in the state of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.
golden-lion-tamarin.story: By the early 1970s only about two hundred golden lion tamarins were left in the wild. In 1972 the Smithsonian's National Zoo brought biologists from Europe, America and Brazil together to save them, and zoo bred tamarins were later returned to Brazil. A census finished in 2023 counted about 4,800 in the wild, the most ever recorded.
golden-lion-tamarin.when: Endangered now, after being moved up from Critically Endangered in 2003.
golden-lion-tamarin.humanRole: Forest clearing for sugar cane, coffee, cattle, logging and towns, and capture for the pet trade, pushed it to the brink.

sources.label: Denver Zoo: Golden lion tamarin fact sheet
Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute: Golden lion tamarin

scimitar-horned-oryx.hook: A desert antelope with sabre curved horns, once gone from the wild and now back in Chad.
scimitar-horned-oryx.imageAlt: A white scimitar oryx with a reddish brown neck and long backward curving horns
scimitar-horned-oryx.what: The scimitar oryx (Oryx dammah) is a desert antelope with a white coat, a reddish brown neck and chest and long horns that curve back like a sabre. Both males and females carry horns. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists it as Endangered.
scimitar-horned-oryx.range: Dry grassland on the southern edge of the Sahara, today wild again in a large reserve in Chad.
scimitar-horned-oryx.story: Overhunting, drought and the loss of grazing to livestock wiped the scimitar oryx out of the wild, and for years it survived only in captivity. Since 2016 Abu Dhabi and Chad have returned captive bred oryx to the wild in Chad, 285 animals in all, and by 2023 the wild herds had grown to more than 600.
scimitar-horned-oryx.when: Endangered since December 2023, when it was moved from Extinct in the Wild to Endangered.
scimitar-horned-oryx.humanRole: Hunting, drought and livestock that ate its grazing drove it out of the wild.

sources.label: Animal Diversity Web: Oryx dammah
Sahara Conservation: the scimitar horned oryx downlisted from Extinct in the Wild to Endangered
Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute: Scimitar oryx

przewalskis-horse.hook: The last truly wild horse, saved in zoos and returned to the steppes of Asia.
przewalskis-horse.imageAlt: A stocky sandy brown Przewalski's horse with a short upright dark mane standing on grass
przewalskis-horse.what: Przewalski's horse (Equus ferus przewalskii) is a stocky wild horse of the Asian steppe, smaller than most domestic horses, with a thick short neck and a short, upright dark mane that it sheds every year. The International Union for Conservation of Nature assesses the whole wild horse species, to which it belongs, and lists it as Endangered.
przewalskis-horse.range: Grassland and semi desert steppe of Mongolia, northern China and Kazakhstan, at reintroduction sites.
przewalskis-horse.story: Przewalski's horses vanished from the wild, and by 1945 fewer than 20 breeding horses were left in the world. Every one of the roughly 1,900 alive today descends from 14 horses caught between 1910 and 1960. Zoo bred herds have since been returned to Mongolia, China and Kazakhstan.
przewalskis-horse.when: Endangered now, wild again only where herds were returned.
przewalskis-horse.humanRole: Competition with people and their livestock, and changes in its environment, pushed it out of the wild.

saiga.hook: A steppe antelope with a big soft drooping nose, brought back in Kazakhstan.
saiga.imageAlt: A saiga antelope with a large drooping nose standing in dry steppe grass
saiga.what: The saiga (Saiga tatarica) is a small antelope of the dry steppe with a large, soft nose that droops over its mouth. Only males carry horns, which are pale and ringed. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists it as Near Threatened.
saiga.range: Dry steppe and semi desert of Central Asia, mainly Kazakhstan, with smaller herds in Kalmykia in Russia and in Mongolia.
saiga.story: Saiga herds crashed, and in 2005 only about 39,000 were left in Kazakhstan. Nearly two decades of work by Kazakhstan, its neighbours, scientists and conservation groups followed, with patrols against poaching, stronger law enforcement and large new protected areas, and the herds there grew to more than 1.9 million.
saiga.when: Near Threatened since December 2023, when it was moved up from Critically Endangered.
saiga.humanRole: Poaching, illegal trade, disease, climate change and new roads, railways and fences still threaten it.

sources.label: Animal Diversity Web: Saiga tatarica

alpine-ibex.hook: A wild mountain goat of the Alps, saved from fewer than 100 animals in one Italian valley.
alpine-ibex.imageAlt: An Alpine ibex with long curved horns standing on a rocky ridge at sunset
alpine-ibex.what: The Alpine ibex (Capra ibex) is a sturdy wild goat of the high Alps with a brown to grey coat. Males are much heavier than females, grow a beard and carry long, curved horns, and both sexes climb steep rock with ease. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists it as Least Concern.
alpine-ibex.range: Steep rocky slopes and alpine meadows of the Alps.
alpine-ibex.story: Hunting with firearms nearly wiped out the Alpine ibex, and the last wild ibex in Switzerland was shot in 1809. Fewer than 100 survived in the Gran Paradiso mountains in Italy at the end of the nineteenth century. Switzerland released its first five ibex in 1911, and today about 18,000 live there and about 40,000 across the Alps.
alpine-ibex.when: Least Concern now, after more than a century of protection and releases.
alpine-ibex.humanRole: Hunting nearly wiped it out, and all of today's ibex come from a small group, so they carry little genetic variety.

northern-elephant-seal.hook: A giant seal hunted until it was thought extinct, now crowding Pacific beaches again.
northern-elephant-seal.imageAlt: Northern elephant seals lying on a sandy beach with a big male rearing up among them
northern-elephant-seal.what: The northern elephant seal (Mirounga angustirostris) is a huge seal of the eastern North Pacific. Adult males are several times heavier than females and have a large, fleshy nose that they can inflate. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists it as Least Concern.
northern-elephant-seal.range: Coastal waters and beaches of the eastern North Pacific, breeding in California and in Baja California, Mexico.
northern-elephant-seal.story: Commercial sealing in the nineteenth century killed so many northern elephant seals that they were thought to be extinct. A few hundred survived in Mexico, and every northern elephant seal alive today descends from them. Under protection the herds grew again, and the California population alone was about 187,000 in 2013.
northern-elephant-seal.when: Least Concern now, breeding again on beaches in the United States and Mexico.
northern-elephant-seal.humanRole: Commercial sealing nearly wiped it out, and today entanglement in fishing gear and collisions with boats threaten it.

indian-rhinoceros.hook: A one horned giant in armour like skin, brought back from fewer than 100 animals.
indian-rhinoceros.imageAlt: An Indian rhinoceros with deep skin folds and a single horn standing in grass
indian-rhinoceros.what: The Indian rhinoceros (Rhinoceros unicornis), also called the greater one horned rhinoceros, is a huge grey brown rhino with deep folds of skin that make it look as if it wears armour. It has a single horn on its snout. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists it as Vulnerable.
indian-rhinoceros.range: Grasslands and river floodplains of northeastern India and southern Nepal, mostly inside national parks.
indian-rhinoceros.story: In the past hundred years the Indian rhinoceros has recovered from fewer than 100 animals to more than 4,000. In March 2025 there were 4,075, with 3,323 in India and 752 in Nepal, helped by better habitat and wildlife corridors.
indian-rhinoceros.when: Vulnerable now, and still guarded closely in its parks.
indian-rhinoceros.humanRole: Hunting and poaching for its horn, and the loss of its grassland to farms, once brought it close to extinction.

sea-otter.hook: The otter with the thickest fur of any animal, hunted almost to the end for it.
sea-otter.imageAlt: Two sea otters floating on their backs in calm water
sea-otter.what: The sea otter (Enhydra lutris) is a large marine otter of the North Pacific. It has no blubber and keeps warm with the densest fur of any mammal. It floats on its back to eat and often cracks shellfish open with a stone. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists it as Endangered.
sea-otter.range: Shallow coastal waters of the North Pacific, from Russia and Japan through Alaska to Canada, with a separate group in central California.
sea-otter.story: Before the fur trade began in the middle of the eighteenth century, there were about 150,000 to 300,000 sea otters. Hunters killed so many that only a few thousand were left when a treaty banned the hunt in 1911. In California a colony of about 50 survived, and it had grown to more than 1,000 by 1972 and to 2,962 by 2019.
sea-otter.when: Endangered now, more than a century after the hunt was banned.
sea-otter.humanRole: Hunting for its fur in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries nearly wiped it out.

american-alligator.hook: A swamp giant once listed as endangered, now common again across the American South.
american-alligator.imageAlt: An American alligator resting at the edge of the water with its dark back showing
american-alligator.what: The American alligator (Alligator mississippiensis) is a large, dark crocodilian of the swamps, rivers and lakes of the southeastern United States. Its tail makes up half of its length. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists it as Least Concern.
american-alligator.range: Freshwater wetlands of the southeastern United States, from North Carolina to Florida and west to central Texas.
american-alligator.story: Poorly regulated hunting led the United States to list the American alligator as endangered across its whole range in 1967. Under federal and state protection it recovered quickly, and in 1987 the government found it was no longer biologically endangered or threatened. It stays on the list only because it looks like the rare American crocodile, so that the crocodile is protected too.
american-alligator.when: Least Concern now, about twenty years after it was listed as endangered.
american-alligator.humanRole: Poorly regulated hunting pushed it down until protection began in 1967.

giant-panda.hook: China's black and white bamboo eater, moved out of the Endangered category in 2016.
giant-panda.imageAlt: A giant panda sitting among green plants and chewing on bamboo
giant-panda.what: The giant panda (Ailuropoda melanoleuca) is a black and white bear of the mountain forests of central China that lives on bamboo. It has strong jaws and broad flat teeth for chewing tough stems, and an enlarged wrist bone works like a thumb to hold them. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists it as Vulnerable.
giant-panda.range: Bamboo forests in the Minshan, Qinling and Qionglai mountains and nearby ranges of central China.
giant-panda.story: China has surveyed its wild pandas about every ten years since the 1970s. The latest surveys found about 1,800 to 2,060 in the wild, and as the numbers grew the International Union for Conservation of Nature moved the giant panda from Endangered to Vulnerable in 2016.
giant-panda.when: Vulnerable since 2016, with wild numbers slowly rising.
giant-panda.humanRole: Loss and breakup of its forests by farms, roads, dams and towns leave many pandas in small groups cut off from each other.

nene.hook: Hawaiʻi's own goose, brought back from about 30 wild birds.
nene.imageAlt: A nēnē goose with a black head, cream cheeks and a streaked buff neck standing on grass
nene.what: The nēnē (Branta sandvicensis), or Hawaiian goose, lives only in the Hawaiian Islands. It has a black face and crown, cream cheeks and a buff neck with black streaks. Its long legs and only partly webbed toes suit walking on lava. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists it as Near Threatened.
nene.range: Grassland, shrubland and lava slopes of the Hawaiian Islands, today mostly on Kauaʻi, Hawaiʻi Island and Maui.
nene.story: Hunting, the loss of its habitat and introduced predators such as mongooses cut the nēnē down to as few as 30 wild birds by the 1950s. Captive breeding, sanctuaries that keep predators out and releases on several islands brought it back, and the 2025 statewide count found about 4,300 birds.
nene.when: Near Threatened now, with most birds on Kauaʻi.
nene.humanRole: Rats, cats, dogs and mongooses still kill nēnē, and many are hit by cars.
